title: QuiX Quantum and Dutch Photonics Consortium Form National Mission for 100+ Qubit Computer - Quantum Computing Report
author: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
text:
European photonic quantum developer QuiX Quantum is leading a three-year national initiative under Phase II of the PhotonDelta National Growth Fund (NGF) Integrated Photonics Programme to build the manufacturing and architectural foundations for a 100+ qubit universal quantum processor. Running through December 2028, the mission coordinates eight Dutch academic and industrial partners across twelve system deliverables, addressing loss, detection, and high-speed control across the photonic quantum stack.

Measurement-based photonic quantum architectures face compounding physical bottlenecks: optical losses across passive routing, non-deterministic photon emission, detector efficiency limits, and electronic latency during active feed-forward switching. Rather than funding isolated component research, the Dutch mission coordinates developers to optimize sub-assemblies against a common error budget necessary for fault-tolerant scaling.

Optical interconnects and control timing represent primary technical hurdles in flight. Minimizing optical loss at the chip boundary is critical to prevent quantum state degradation before photons enter the processing core. Concurrently, reducing control latency ensures that feed-forward logic can dynamically reconfigure phase shifters and optical switches in real time before traveling photons reach subsequent interferometric stages.

The national mission aligns with concurrent international supply-chain initiatives backed by PhotonDelta. Under the recent Netherlands–Taiwan TechBridge framework, QuiX Quantum partnered with Brillink to develop high-efficiency SPAD arrays, while consortium partner MicroAlign teamed with Largan to engineer mass-producible, ultra-low-loss fiber-array connections. The coordinated programs bridge QuiX Quantum’s delivery of universal hardware to the German Aerospace Center (DLR QCI) and inform the company’s loss-tolerant Dedalo architecture, targeting logical-qubit demonstrations between 2028 and 2030.
